q: Scientists once thought male humpback whales sang only on their breeding grounds. Where else have recordings caught them singing?
explain: Decades of underwater recordings show humpback males also sing on their feeding grounds and while migrating between feeding and breeding areas.

source.publisher: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries
source.title: Unraveling Mysteries of Humpback Whale Song at Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary

source2.publisher: NOAA Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary
source2.title: Baleen Whales

searchNote: NOAA sanctuaries article says song was once thought limited to breeding grounds, but 50 years of recordings show males also sing on feeding grounds and during migration.

q: In group bubble-net feeding, how do humpback whales finally catch the fish trapped by their bubbles?
choices: They lunge upward through the net
They scoop them off the seafloor
They herd them onto the beach
explain: Curtains of rising bubbles bunch the fish together. The whales then push them toward the surface and lunge up through the circular net to engulf them.
searchNote: NOAA species page describes group coordinated bubble net feeding: bubble curtains condense prey, fish are pushed toward the surface and engulfed as whales lunge upward through the circular net.

q: Besides bubbles, which body part have humpback whales been seen using to herd and corral prey?
explain: NOAA notes humpbacks corral prey using bubbles, sounds, the seafloor and even their huge pectoral fins, a tactic researchers have called pectoral herding.

source2.title: Pectoral herding: an innovative tactic for humpback whale foraging

searchNote: NOAA species page lists bubbles, sounds, the seafloor and pectoral fins as ways humpbacks herd, corral and disorient prey; a PMC paper is titled 'Pectoral herding: an innovative tactic for humpback whale foraging'.

q: Baleen, the bristly plates some whales use to filter food, is made of the same material as what?
explain: Baleen is made of keratin, the same tough but flexible protein found in our fingernails and hair.

source2.title: Baleen whales: Filter feeding explained

searchNote: Smithsonian Ocean says baleen is strong but flexible and made of keratin, the same substance as fingernails; NHM London says the same protein makes our nails and hair.

q: The male narwhal's long spiral tusk is a type of tooth. Which kind?
explain: Researchers traced the tusk to the maxillary bone, where mammal canine teeth form, showing it is a canine rather than an incisor.

source.title: For a dentist, the narwhal's smile is a mystery of evolution

source2.title: Curious collections: two-tusked narwhal

searchNote: Smithsonian results say the tusk is one of a pair of canine teeth; it was identified as a canine, not an incisor, because it originates in the maxillary bone. NHM London also calls it a canine tooth.

q: Which narwhals usually grow the long, visible tusk?
explain: The tusk usually erupts in males. In females it rarely does; they typically keep two small teeth embedded in the upper jaw.

source.title: Why a Tusk? The real-life unicorns of the sea and the tusks that make them famous

source2.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
source2.title: Narwhal: Revealing an Arctic Legend

searchNote: Smithsonian results describe the tusk as the male narwhal's; a tusk rarely erupts in females, which instead have two small embedded teeth in the upper jaw. Verifier: confirm which Smithsonian page carries the female detail.

q: What makes the narwhal's tusk unusual compared with most teeth?
choices: It grows from the lower jaw
Nerves inside connect to its outer surface
It is made of solid bone
explain: Nerves in the tusk's core connect to the outside through millions of tiny fluid-filled channels, which is why researchers study it as a sensory organ.

source.title: Researchers map pathway of narwhal's sensitive tusk to brain

source2.title: Why a Tusk? The real-life unicorns of the sea and the tusks that make them famous

searchNote: Smithsonian results say the tusk's inner nerve system connects directly to the outside, with an estimated 10 million fluid-filled tubules from base to tip; the tusk originates in the upper (maxillary) bone.

q: Unlike most whales, a beluga can turn its head up, down and sideways. Why?
choices: Its neck vertebrae are not fused
It has no neck bones at all
Its skull rests on a fat cushion
explain: Most whales have fused neck vertebrae, but a beluga's are separate, giving it a flexible neck that can move its head in several directions.
searchNote: NOAA beluga page: unlike most whales, belugas' cervical vertebrae are not fused, letting them move the head up, down and side to side.

q: Why did sailors long ago nickname beluga whales 'sea canaries'?
explain: Belugas are very vocal. Their squeals, squeaks and chirps earned them the old sailors' nickname 'sea canaries'.
searchNote: NOAA says belugas squeal, squeak and chirp, which is why sailors long ago called them sea canaries.

q: A beluga's rounded forehead, called the melon, is unusually flexible. What does that let the whale do?
explain: The beluga's melon can change shape, which lets the whale make a range of different facial expressions.

source2.title: Beluga Whales

searchNote: Beluga search results said the bulbous forehead, called a melon, is very flexible, allowing many different facial expressions. Verifier: confirm the Georgia Aquarium page (or Shedd's belugas page) carries this.

q: How does a gray whale usually feed?
choices: Rolling on its side to suck up seafloor mud
explain: A gray whale turns on its side and sucks in sediment from the seafloor, then strains out the mud and water through its baleen, keeping the small animals inside.

source2.title: Eastern Pacific Gray Whale

searchNote: NOAA describes the gray whale turning on its side and scooping the top few inches of seafloor sediment; baleen holds back food while mud and water pass out.

q: In its Arctic feeding grounds, what is the gray whale's favorite food?
explain: Gray whales feeding in the Arctic mainly target amphipods, tiny crustaceans that live in the seafloor sediment the whales suck up.

source.title: Sentinels of Change: Gray Whales in the Arctic

searchNote: NOAA Arctic feature describes amphipods as the gray whales' favorite food in the Arctic.

q: About how long do studies suggest a bowhead whale may live?
explain: New ways of estimating age suggest bowheads may live for more than 200 years, making them the longest-lived marine mammal known.

source.title: What is the longest-lived marine mammal?

source2.title: Bowhead Whale

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Service fact page on the longest-lived marine mammal is about the bowhead; NOAA's species page says studies suggest bowheads may live over 200 years.

q: What can a bowhead whale do with its huge, thick skull?
choices: Break through sea ice to breathe
explain: Bowheads live in icy Arctic waters, and their large, thick skulls let them break through sea ice to reach air. NOAA says ice about 8 inches thick.

source2.title: 5 Icebreakers About Bowhead Whales

searchNote: NOAA species page: the bowhead's large, thick skull allows it to break through 8-inch-thick sea ice; a Sea Grant article says it uses its head to break ice from below to breathe.

q: How many blowholes does a baleen whale, such as a humpback, have?
explain: Baleen whales have two blowholes side by side, while toothed whales such as dolphins and sperm whales have just one.

source2.title: Whales and Dolphins - Smithsonian Ocean Portal

searchNote: NOAA whale anatomy resource: Mysticeti (baleen whales) have two blowholes, while toothed whales (Odontoceti) have only one.

q: About how much of a sperm whale's total body length is taken up by its head?
explain: A sperm whale's enormous, boxy head makes up about one-third of its body length.
searchNote: NOAA sperm whale page says the head is about one-third of the total body length.

q: Remains found in sperm whale stomachs show they eat which deep-sea animal?
explain: Giant squid beaks have turned up in sperm whale stomachs, and large sucker scars on stranded whales suggest the squid fight back.

source.title: How Big is the Giant Squid? - Smithsonian Ocean Portal

source2.title: Giant Squid vs. Sperm Whale

searchNote: Smithsonian says giant squid beaks and other undigested remains have been found in sperm whale stomachs; stranded sperm whales carry large sucker scars.

q: The killer whale, or orca, is the largest member of which animal family?
explain: Despite its name, the orca belongs to Delphinidae, the oceanic dolphin family, and is its largest member.

source2.title: What's the difference between dolphins and porpoises?

searchNote: NOAA: the killer whale is the largest member of the Delphinidae family, or dolphins; NOAA Ocean Service says the orca is actually the largest member of the dolphin family.

q: In the Pacific Northwest, what do 'resident' killer whales mainly eat?
explain: Resident killer whales in the Pacific Northwest eat fish, mainly salmon, while the Bigg's (transient) killer whales in the same waters hunt marine mammals.

source2.title: New killer whale species: Bigg's and resident killer whales

searchNote: NOAA says one Pacific Northwest ecotype eats fish, mainly salmon; transient (Bigg's) killer whales prey on marine mammals, most often harbor seals in one study.

q: What mainly determines the diet of each killer whale ecotype (a distinct regional type of orca)?
explain: Killer whale groups pass down their hunting tactics, so culture largely decides whether an ecotype specializes in fish, seals or other prey.
searchNote: Search summary quoted NOAA: diet is primarily determined by the culture (learned hunting tactics) of each ecotype. Verifier: confirm this sentence is on the species page.

q: Compared with fish-eating 'resident' killer whales, how often do mammal-hunting 'transient' killer whales use echolocation clicks?
explain: One study found residents produced echolocation click trains about 27 times more often than the marine-mammal-eating transients.

source.title: Killer Whale (Orcinus orca) Predation of Marine Mammals Bibliography

searchNote: NOAA bibliography entry: resident killer whales produced trains of sonar clicks on average 4% of the time, 27 times more often than marine-mammal-eating transients.

q: What makes the rough patches, or callosities, on a right whale's head look white?
explain: Callosities are patches of rough skin on an otherwise dark whale. They look white because they are covered in whale lice, tiny crustaceans called cyamids.

source2.title: A Tale of a Right Whale - Smithsonian Ocean Portal

searchNote: Search results: right whales have knobby white patches of rough skin that appear white because of whale lice (cyamids) covering the otherwise black skin.

q: How do researchers tell individual North Atlantic right whales apart?
choices: By the pattern of callosities on their heads
By the pitch of their songs
explain: Each right whale has a unique pattern of callosities, rough skin patches on its head, that researchers match against photo catalogs, much like fingerprints.
searchNote: NOAA: callosities occur in unique patterns on North Atlantic right whales and help researchers identify and track individuals via photo catalogs.

q: What do the whale lice living on a right whale's callosities mainly feed on?
explain: Whale lice are small crustaceans that eat algae settling on the callosities, causing only minor damage to the whale's skin.
searchNote: Smithsonian whale lice page: the cyamid amphipods on callosities eat algae that settles there and cause only minor skin damage.

q: How do porpoise teeth typically differ from the teeth of most dolphins?
explain: Most dolphins have cone-shaped teeth, while porpoise teeth are flattened and spade-shaped, one way to tell the two apart up close.

source.title: What's the difference between dolphins and porpoises?

source2.title: What's the Difference Between Dolphins and Porpoises?

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Service: most dolphins have cone-shaped teeth while porpoise teeth are flattened; NOAA Fisheries calls porpoise teeth flat and spade shaped.

q: What dorsal fin shape is typical of porpoises?
explain: Porpoises usually have triangular dorsal fins, while most dolphins have curved, sickle-like fins, though NOAA notes there are exceptions.

source.title: What's the Difference Between Dolphins and Porpoises?

searchNote: NOAA Fisheries: dolphins have hooked or curved (falcate) dorsal fins like a sickle; porpoises have triangular dorsal fins.

q: Which dolphin is nicknamed the 'hookfin porpoise' for its large, curved dorsal fin?
explain: The Pacific white-sided dolphin's big, hooked fin earned it the nickname 'hookfin porpoise', even though it is a dolphin, not a porpoise.
searchNote: NOAA species page: the Pacific white-sided dolphin is nicknamed the hookfin porpoise for its large curved fin, but it is not technically a porpoise.

q: Where does the vaquita, the world's smallest porpoise, live?
explain: The vaquita lives only in the northern Gulf of California, Mexico, giving it one of the smallest ranges of any marine mammal.
searchNote: NOAA: the vaquita (Phocoena sinus) is the world's smallest porpoise and lives only in the northern Gulf of California, mostly east of San Felipe, Baja California.

q: What is the main threat to the endangered vaquita?
explain: Vaquitas get tangled and drown in gillnets, especially illegal nets set for a large fish called the totoaba.

source2.title: Endangered Vaquita Remain Genetically Healthy Even in Low Numbers, New Analysis Shows

searchNote: Smithsonian and NOAA results: the decline is due to bycatch in gillnets, especially an illegal fishery for the totoaba; NOAA genetic study says recovery is possible if illegal gillnetting stops.

q: What is a bottlenose dolphin's 'signature whistle'?
choices: A call that warns of sharks
A song that only males sing
A call that identifies the individual
explain: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own learned whistle, and other dolphins can recognize who is calling from the whistle's shape alone.

source.title: Signature whistle shape conveys identity information to bottlenose dolphins - PMC

searchNote: Study shows bottlenose dolphins extract identity information from signature whistles even with voice features removed; whistles are learned and individually distinctive.

q: When their calves are nearby, how do bottlenose dolphin mothers change their signature whistles?
explain: Rather like human baby talk, dolphin mothers in a long-term study whistled with higher maximum pitches and a wider pitch range when with their calves.

source.title: Bottlenose dolphin mothers modify signature whistles in ...

searchNote: Only the result title was shown ('Bottlenose dolphin mothers modify signature whistles in...'). Verifier: confirm the paper reports higher maximum frequency and wider frequency range when calves are present.

q: How do dolphins manage to sleep while still surfacing to breathe?
choices: They rest one half of the brain at a time
They hold their breath for hours
They sleep only on the seafloor
explain: In unihemispheric sleep, one half of the brain rests while the other stays alert, letting dolphins keep moving, surface for air and stay watchful.

source2.title: Sleep in Aquatic Mammals - PMC - NIH

searchNote: Search results: dolphins sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time (unihemispheric slow-wave sleep); the awake side lets them surface for air and stay vigilant.

q: In one study, how long did bottlenose dolphins keep up alert echolocation without a break or signs of mental fatigue?
explain: Bottlenose dolphins in the study kept detecting targets with echolocation for 15 days straight without signs of cognitive impairment.

source.title: Dolphins Can Maintain Vigilant Behavior through Echolocation for 15 Days without Interruption or Cognitive Impairment

searchNote: Paper title states dolphins maintained vigilant behavior through echolocation for 15 days without interruption or cognitive impairment. Verifier: confirm species is bottlenose dolphin.

q: Some bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia, carry sea sponges on their snouts. Why?
choices: To carry food to their calves
To protect them while probing the seafloor
explain: A dolphin breaks off a cone-shaped sponge and wears it over its beak, apparently as protection while it probes the sandy seafloor for hidden fish.

source2.title: Why Do Dolphins Carry Sponges?

searchNote: Results: a dolphin breaks a sponge off the seafloor and wears it over its closed rostrum to probe the substrate for fish; dolphins seeking burrowing prey benefit from protective sponges.

q: How is sponge tool use mainly passed on among Shark Bay bottlenose dolphins?
explain: Genetic work shows sponging stays almost entirely within one family line, passed from mother to daughter, which researchers called the first known material culture in a marine mammal.

source.title: Cultural transmission of tool use in bottlenose dolphins - PMC

searchNote: Paper found sponging shows almost exclusive vertical social transmission within a single matriline from mother to female offspring, called the first case of material culture in a marine mammal.

q: What does a Dall's porpoise create when it surfaces quickly while swimming fast?
explain: Dall's porpoises surface so briskly that they throw up a 'rooster tail' of water spray, a trademark of the species.

source2.title: Dall's Porpoise - Phocoenoides Dalli - Kenai Fjords National Park

searchNote: NOAA: Dall's porpoises briskly surface while swimming, creating a rooster tail of water spray that is a unique characteristic of the species.

q: What can scientists learn from the layers in a baleen whale's earwax plug?
choices: The depth of its deepest dive
explain: Earwax builds up in layers over a baleen whale's life, a bit like tree rings, so a plug from a museum specimen can reveal the whale's age.

source.title: Whale Earwax: What You Can Learn From Strange Collections

searchNote: Only the result title was shown. Verifier: confirm the Smithsonian page says earwax plugs form layers that can be counted to estimate a whale's age.
